title: Finance & Cost Management
sequence: Planning (estimates, budget, baseline, funding strategy); Monitor and Control Finances then runs through Executing and Monitoring & Controlling.

header.html: Process domain (41%) · Task 6 Plan and manage finance — analyze project financial needs · quantify risk and contingency financial allocations · plan spend tracking throughout the project life cycle · plan financial reporting · anticipate future finance challenges · monitor financial variations and work with the governance process · manage financial reserves

Topic 21 (reserves in depth, EMV, the budget buildup diagram) · Topic 10 (value metrics: NPV, IRR, payback, ROI, sunk costs) · Topic 14 (estimating techniques, basis of estimates) · Topic 22 (contract types) · Topic 28 (reporting) · Topic 34 (more worked earned value calculations)

Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Purpose of the domain: use and allocate money well so that the project delivers maximum value. The value of financial measurement is not collecting the data but using it in conversations and decisions.

Term Meaning
Value definition / maximization Value can be tangible (ROI, IRR, payback, ROA, ROACE) or intangible (customer satisfaction, innovation, social and environmental value). The domain aims at value, not only low cost; sometimes spending more is right because value depends on delivery by a date (Topic 10)
Funding How the project gets its money: internal budgets, customer contracts, grants, crowdfunding and so on
Financial constraints The budget is the main one but not the only: CapEx (investment in property, plant, buildings, technology, equipment) versus OpEx (day-to-day running costs: wages, rent, utilities, advertising), internal versus external personnel, funds tied to a fiscal year (cannot carry over), grants with conditions. Agile budgets may be allocated quarterly and revised each quarter
Cost estimate A quantitative assessment of the likely cost of the resources needed for an activity, based on the information known at a given time
Project budget Built up from estimates, contingency reserve and management reserve, depending on organizational practice (two scenarios below)
Cost baseline The approved time-phased project budget, excluding management reserve (in one variant also excluding contingency), changeable only through formal change control and used for comparison with actuals
Performance measurement baseline (PMB) The integrated scope, schedule and cost baselines used to measure and control execution
Budget at completion (BAC) The sum of all budgets established for the work (the total planned value)
Project funding requirements Total and periodic funding derived from the cost baseline (including contingency); total funds = cost baseline + management reserve; funding is often incremental and uneven
Reserve A provision in the plan to mitigate cost or schedule risk, usually named by type (contingency, management)
Cost measurement Different stakeholders recognize cost at different points: when the decision is made or committed, when the order is placed, when the item is delivered, or when the cost is incurred or recorded; decide which applies
Life cycle cost Every project decision affects later cost of use, maintenance and support; for example, cutting design reviews may lower project cost but raise the product's operating cost
Revenue forecast A projection of expected income from sales or services; used in planning and decisions

2The Four Finance Processes

Process Focus area Purpose Key outputs Decision tools
Plan Financial Management Planning (once or at defined points) Define how revenues and expenses will be estimated, budgeted, managed, monitored and controlled, aligned with objectives and strategy Financial management plan, funding strategy Expert judgment, alternative analysis, meetings
Estimate Costs Planning (periodic) Approximate the cost of resources needed to complete the work Cost estimates, basis of estimates Analogous, parametric, bottom-up, multipoint estimating; reserve analysis; cost of quality; alternative analysis; voting
Develop Budget Planning (once or at defined points) Aggregate activity or work package estimates into an authorized cost baseline Cost baseline, project funding requirements Cost aggregation, reserve analysis, historical information review, funding limit reconciliation, financing
Monitor and Control Finances Monitoring & Controlling (throughout) Track spending, update financial records, manage cost baseline and revenue forecast changes, keep the project financially viable Work performance information, cost and revenue forecasts, change requests, funding proposals, plan and baseline updates Earned value analysis, trend analysis, reserve analysis, TCPI, PMIS

3Plan Financial Management

3.1 The financial management plan

Describes how costs will be planned, structured and controlled:

Element What it defines
Units of measure Staff hours, days, weeks, quantities, or currency lump sums
Level of precision Rounding (for example US$995.59 to US$1,000)
Level of accuracy Acceptable range (for example ±10%), possibly including contingency
Links to organizational procedures The WBS framework; the control account is the WBS component used for cost accounting, with a code linked to the organization's accounting system
Control thresholds Variance limits (usually % deviation from baseline) that trigger action
Rules of performance measurement EVM rules: where control accounts are measured, techniques (weighted milestones, fixed formula, percent complete), how the EAC is calculated to cross-check the bottom-up EAC
Reporting formats Format and frequency of cost reports
Additional details Strategic funding choices; procedure for currency exchange fluctuations; procedure for recording project costs

3.2 ECO enabler: analyze project financial needs

Question Notes
How much money, and when? Funding requirements from the cost baseline: total and periodic, often incremental and uneven
From where? Choose a funding strategy (diagram): fixed or reallocated internal budgets, lump sum, incremental disbursement (by phase or milestone), external investment, government or NGO grants, crowdfunding, client contract. Financing (external funds) may come with the funder's requirements
Under what constraints? CapEx or OpEx, fiscal-year limits, funding limits, conditions on grants or investors
What value is expected? Business case, benefits and financial measures (NPV, IRR, payback, ROI, cost-benefit analysis; Topic 10)
What will it cost over the product's life? Include operating and maintenance cost in trade-offs
What outside factors apply? Currency, inflation, cost of financing, regulation (for example SOX or GDPR for financial data integrity and security), contract type

Funding proposals: dedicated requests for funding (before the project or for a phase) built from estimated costs and reserves as part of a business value proposition.

3.3 ECO enabler: plan spend tracking throughout the life cycle

  • Decide when cost is recognized (committed, ordered, delivered, incurred) and align it with the accounting system through control accounts.
  • Use a time-phased budget and agreed thresholds; set EVM rules (percent complete, weighted milestones, fixed formula).
  • Adaptive: track spend per iteration against delivered value and the budget, and apply continuous funding assessment; quarterly budgets are revised each quarter. Contracts should follow the iterative cadence. Quarterly totals alone arrive too late.

3.4 ECO enabler: plan financial reporting

  • Define formats, frequency and audiences (sponsor, governance bodies, finance, regulators) in the financial management plan; link them to the information requirements found in planning (Topic 14, section 5).
  • Support governance: if the board asks for earned value data, adapt the reporting to provide it; the project does not decide whether the requirement is needed.
  • Include forecasts (the EAC is documented and communicated), variance against thresholds, and the status of reserves.

4Estimate Costs

  • Costs are estimated for all resources charged to the project: labor, materials, equipment, services and facilities, plus special categories such as an inflation allowance, cost of financing and contingency. Estimating only labor is a gap (Topic 14, section 8).
  • Estimates may be shown at activity level or in summary, in currency or in staff hours (to remove currency effects). They are refined as the project progresses, and accuracy improves.
  • Techniques: expert judgment, analogous, parametric, bottom-up, multipoint (formulas and use in Topic 14), plus the constructive cost model (COCOMO) for software effort, time and cost from size inputs; voting and alternative analysis.
  • Alternatives to consider: make versus buy, buy versus lease, sharing resources, to reach the optimal cost.
  • Cost of quality (CoQ):
Cost of conformance (money spent to avoid failures) Cost of nonconformance (money spent because of failures)
Prevention: training, documented processes, equipment, time to do it right Internal failure (found by the project): rework, scrap
Appraisal: testing, inspections, destructive-testing loss External failure (found by the customer): liabilities, warranty work, lost business

There is an optimal CoQ where extra prevention and appraisal stop paying off. Prevention costs less than appraisal and failure (Topic 18).

  • Outputs: cost estimates and the basis of estimates (assumptions, constraints, ranges, confidence level).

5Develop Budget

  • Cost aggregation: work package estimates are summed to control accounts, then to the project total.
  • Reserve analysis and historical information review refine the budget; reserves are added according to the plan.
  • Funding limit reconciliation: when planned spending exceeds a funding limit, reschedule work (imposed date constraints) to level out the rate of spending or obtain more funding.
  • Cost baseline: the approved time-phased budget (an S-curve); changed only through formal change control. Project funding requirements follow from it.

Two budget buildup scenarios (PMBOK 8 Figure 2-25; diagram in Topic 21):

Reserves managed implicitly Reserves managed explicitly
Initial budget Work cost estimates + contingency reserve + management reserve Work cost estimates only
Cost baseline Includes contingency (excludes management reserve) Excludes both reserves
Where reserves live Inside the budget Tracked and managed separately

6Quantify Risk and Contingency Allocations; Manage Financial Reserves (ECO)

Contingency reserve Management reserve
Covers Known risks with active response strategies (known-unknowns) Unforeseen work within scope (unknown-unknowns), not specific risks
Where Time or money in the schedule or cost baseline (usually in the initial budget; may sit outside per organizational preference) In addition to the baseline; never part of the cost baseline
Who releases Per the reserve protocols in the risk management plan Usually senior management; in some organizations the PM or team
Sizing Percentage, fixed amount, or quantitative analysis; at activity or project level; shrinks as risks pass A management decision

How to quantify contingency:

  • Assess risks (Topic 21), then size the reserve from expected monetary values or simulation. Example Beyond PMBOK 8summing EMVs for accepted risks: risks with EMVs of $30,000, $20,000 and $20,000 suggest a contingency of about $70,000, adjusted for dependencies and confidence level.
  • Identify contingency clearly in the cost documentation; do not hide it in estimates.
  • Reserve analysis compares remaining risk with remaining reserve to judge sufficiency.

How to manage reserves:

  • Use contingency when identified risks occur; reduce or release it as risks pass.
  • Use management reserve only for unforeseen in-scope work, through the approval path set by the organization. Beyond PMBOK 8 Using it normally requires a change request so the baseline reflects the new authorization.
  • Reserve burning faster than progress is a governance signal: reassess adequacy against remaining risks and tell the sponsor. Do not quietly top up from management reserve (Topic 21).
  • Tailoring: small projects and government projects (more accountability, risk aversion) often hold larger buffers; the sponsor and stakeholders may set the level.

7Monitor and Control Finances

What it does: tracks expenditures, updates financial records, adjusts the cost baseline and revenue forecasts through change control, performs variance analysis against thresholds, and implements corrective action so the project remains financially viable and benefits are realized.

7.1 Earned value analysis (PMBOK 8 Table 5-1)

Measure Formula Reading
PV (planned value) Authorized budget assigned to scheduled work What should be done by now
EV (earned value) Budget authorized for the work actually completed (never more than the PV for a component) Work done, in budget terms
AC (actual cost) Realized cost of the work performed Definition must match what PV and EV include
CV EV − AC Positive: under budget; negative: over budget
SV EV − PV Positive: ahead; negative: behind
CPI EV ÷ AC Above 1: under budget; below 1: over budget
SPI EV ÷ PV Above 1: ahead; below 1: behind
EAC See below Expected total cost at completion
ETC EAC − AC (or a bottom-up reestimate) Expected cost to finish
VAC BAC − EAC Positive: under budget at completion
TCPI (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC), or (BAC − EV) ÷ (EAC − AC) Efficiency needed on remaining work: above 1 harder, 1 same, below 1 easier

Which EAC (PMBOK 8):

Situation Formula
Current cost performance will continue EAC = BAC ÷ CPI
Future work will go at the planned rate (the variance was a one-off) EAC = AC + (BAC − EV)
The original plan is no longer valid EAC = AC + bottom-up ETC
Both cost and schedule performance affect the remaining work EAC = AC + [(BAC − EV) ÷ (CPI × SPI)]

Worked example: BAC = 100, PV = 50, EV = 40, AC = 48 at month 6. CV = −8, SV = −10, CPI = 0.83, SPI = 0.80. EAC = 100 ÷ 0.833 = 120; ETC = 120 − 48 = 72; VAC = −20; TCPI (BAC) = 60 ÷ 52 = 1.15. If a TCPI that high is unrealistic, forecast with the EAC and request approval for a new baseline through change control.

Adaptive EVM (PMBOK 8): effort in story points. PV = points planned to date (usually to iteration end); EV = points of stories done in the same period; AC = the team's cost for the iteration (from working hours).

7.2 Responding to a financial variance

  1. Compare with thresholds in the financial management plan.
  2. Find the cause (root cause analysis); consider schedule performance too (an over-budget, ahead-of-schedule result may be paid-for speed).
  3. Forecast with the appropriate EAC; update revenue and cost forecasts; check TCPI.
  4. Evaluate options: corrective action, scope or quality trade-offs through change control, use of reserves per protocol, schedule changes, funding proposals, additional funds.
  5. Escalate through governance when thresholds or authority are exceeded; bring options and a recommendation. If no threshold exists for a decision above your spending authority, work with the sponsor to define it rather than inferring one.
  6. Update the baseline and plans only through approved change requests; communicate the forecast to stakeholders.

8Anticipate Future Finance Challenges (ECO)

Challenge Response
Inflation and exchange rates Include an inflation allowance; follow the plan's procedure for currency fluctuation (allowances, fixed-rate contracting, hedging through the organization's finance function)
Resource cost and availability Constraints raise cost (higher wages, training, expedited shipping, rental surcharges, late-delivery penalties); plan resources early (Topic 19)
Contract type Make-or-buy and contract type shift cost risk: fixed-price moves cost overrun risk to the seller; time and materials keeps it with the buyer (Topic 22)
Funding limits and timing Funding limit reconciliation; funding proposals; incremental disbursement
Regulation and compliance cost Controls such as SOX or GDPR; compliance threats are risks (Topic 23)
Scope, schedule and risk effects Changes ripple to cost; keep the forecast current (Topics 15, 16, 21)
Life cycle cost Weigh operating and maintenance costs, not only project cost
Revenue shortfall Track revenue forecasts and the business case (Topic 10)

Tools: trend analysis, forecasting, what-if scenarios, reserve analysis, EAC and TCPI, and the risk register.

9Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Budgeting Full budget and cost baseline up front; contingency and management reserve Budget by quarter or increment, revised each quarter; continuous funding assessment Baseline for the fixed envelope; incremental funding for iterative parts
Spend curve S-curve over the project Flatter spend curve; steady burn per iteration Mixed
Funding Lump sum or milestone disbursement Incremental disbursement tied to value delivered Both
Tracking Time-phased budget; EVM against the PMB; CPI, SPI, EAC Spend per iteration vs delivered value; EVM in story points Both
Change Cost baseline changes through change control Backlog reprioritization within the budget envelope Change control for the envelope only
Contracts Fixed-price or cost-based as risk suits Contracts aligned to iteration cadence; frequent adjustment Mixed

10Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

Tailoring considerations (PMBOK 8 §2.4.3):

Factor Effect
Product Regulated industries (finance, pharmaceuticals) need formal financial controls (SOX, GDPR) and multi-phase tracking
Development approach Iterative work flattens the spend curve; use time-phased budgeting and continuous funding assessment
Procurement strategy Make-or-buy and contract type (fixed-price, time and materials) determine risk distribution and cost certainty; tailor financial processes to the strategy
Value definition Varies by organization
Resource availability Constraints raise actual and forecast costs

PMBOK 8 examples: (1) an adaptive project needs frequent budget and contract adjustment, structured to follow the iteration cadence; (2) a small project has little financial flexibility, so contingency and management reserves are crucial; (3) a government project needs more fiscal accountability and a larger reserve buffer, influenced by sponsors and stakeholders.

Interactions: finance directly affects and is affected by governance, scope and schedule; stakeholders and risk also influence it. The primary goal is maximum value linked to strategy.

Check results (Table 2-8):

Outcome Check
Contribution to business objectives ROI, NPV, IRR, cost-benefit analysis, KPIs, OKRs, CapEx, OpEx
Within or below budget Variance analysis (CV, CPI); vendor financial targets in the signed contract
Deliverables validated according to plan EVM and other organizational metrics
Value created (investment or other value) Metrics matching the project success criteria
Financial visibility Trend analysis, graphical analysis, forecasting

11Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Forecast total cost with the EAC, not the BAC and not the SPI.
  2. CPI is cost efficiency; SPI is schedule efficiency. Do not mix them, and read them together (CPI below 1 with SPI above 1 means schedule recovered at a cost).
  3. Choose the EAC formula by the assumption: typical variance (BAC ÷ CPI), one-off variance (AC + BAC − EV), invalid plan (bottom-up), cost and schedule both matter (CPI × SPI).
  4. Cost baseline excludes management reserve; changes only through change control; the PMB is scope + schedule + cost baselines.
  5. Contingency vs management reserve: identified risks vs unknown-unknowns; reserves are released per protocol, management reserve usually by senior management.
  6. Reserve burning fast is a governance signal; reassess and inform the sponsor, do not quietly refill.
  7. Report to governance in the form it requires (for example earned value) and escalate variances beyond thresholds with options.
  8. No threshold defined for a decision above your authority: define it with the sponsor; do not infer it.
  9. Do not bury an overrun. Forecast early, show options, request funding through change control and governance.
  10. Estimate all resource types (equipment, materials, facilities, fees, inflation, financing), not only labor.
  11. Consider life cycle cost, not just project cost; the cheapest build can be the costliest product.
  12. Funding limits are respected: reconcile by rescheduling or obtaining more funding; do not overspend and explain later.
  13. Agile finance: spend per iteration against delivered value, quarterly budget revision; do not report only at quarter end.
  14. Sunk costs are ignored in continue-or-stop decisions (Topic 10).
  15. Approved scope changes update the cost baseline (and funding requirements) through change control; contingency is for risks, not for scope growth.
  16. A TCPI far above 1 signals the BAC is no longer viable: forecast with the EAC and seek approval of a revised baseline.

12Exam Q&A

12.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A project has BAC 200,000, EV 80,000 and AC 100,000. The overrun came from a one-off supplier error that has been corrected, so the rest of the work will cost what was planned. What is the best EAC?

  • A300,000, adding the whole BAC on top of the actual cost so far
  • B200,000, because the original budget at completion still stands
  • C250,000, using BAC divided by the current CPI of 0.8 as if performance continues
  • D220,000, using AC plus the remaining planned work (BAC minus EV)
Show the answer

Answer: D. When the variance was a one-off and future work will go at the planned rate, EAC equals AC plus (BAC minus EV): 100,000 plus 120,000 gives 220,000. BAC divided by CPI assumes the poor performance continues, and the other figures ignore either the overrun or the work remaining.

S2A project has BAC 500, EV 200 and AC 250. What is the TCPI based on BAC, and what does it suggest?

  • A1.20: the remaining work must be performed 20% more efficiently than planned
  • B0.80: the project is over budget and the remaining work can be done less efficiently
  • C1.25: the remaining work needs 25% fewer resources than planned
  • D0.83: the remaining work can be done 17% less efficiently than planned
Show the answer

Answer: A. TCPI equals (BAC minus EV) divided by (BAC minus AC): 300 divided by 250 gives 1.20, meaning the remaining work must be done 20% more efficiently, and if that is unrealistic the project should forecast with the EAC and seek a new baseline. 0.80 is the CPI, and the other values invert or misread the ratio.

S3In a quarterly-funded agile program, planned spending in the third quarter exceeds the funding limit by 300,000. What is the usual way to reconcile this?

  • ACut the quality of the deliverables until the third-quarter spending fits the limit
  • BRaise the funding limit in the plan, since the work has already been approved
  • CReschedule work to level out the rate of spending, or obtain additional funding
  • DMove the 300,000 into the management reserve so that it is no longer counted
Show the answer

Answer: C. Funding limit reconciliation reschedules work through imposed date constraints to even out spending, or secures more funding through the proper path. Editing the limit, cutting quality or hiding the amount in reserve does not respect the funding constraint.

S4On a hybrid program, the project tracks cost when purchase orders are placed, while finance records it when invoices are paid, and the two reports never match. What should the project manager do?

  • ASwitch to finance's view and stop tracking commitments altogether
  • BAgree with finance when cost is recognized and align the tracking to it
  • CKeep the project's own view, because the PM is accountable for commitments
  • DReport both figures to the sponsor without explaining the difference
Show the answer

Answer: B. Stakeholders may recognize cost when it is committed, ordered, delivered or incurred, so the plan states which applies and links to the accounting system through control accounts. Choosing one view, dropping commitments or reporting both unexplained keeps the confusion.

S5Funds tied to the fiscal year will expire in three weeks, and 400,000 remains unspent because a vendor deliverable is late. What should the project manager do?

  • AOrder extra equipment now so the funds are used before they expire
  • BWork with the sponsor and finance to re-phase the budget or seek a carry-over
  • CMove the 400,000 into the project's management reserve for next year
  • DLet the funds lapse and absorb the later costs from the contingency
Show the answer

Answer: B. Funds tied to a fiscal year cannot simply carry over, so the project manager works with the sponsor and finance to re-phase the budget or obtain approval to carry over. Spending on unneeded items is wasteful and unethical, and shifting funds into reserve or relying on contingency misuses them.

S6The scrum team proposes dropping design reviews from the definition of done to save 50,000 now, but the reviews would reduce the maintenance cost of the finished product. How should the project manager proceed?

  • APresent the trade-off including life cycle cost to the sponsor for a decision
  • BReject the proposal, since reviews are always required on a project
  • CAccept the saving, because the project is judged on its own budget
  • DApprove the cut and track the extra maintenance in a separate report
Show the answer

Answer: A. Every project decision affects later cost of use and support, so the trade-off is judged on life cycle cost and the sponsor decides with the full picture. Judging only the project budget, rejecting by rule or approving and separating the consequence ignores that effect.

S7A contract is priced in euros while the project is funded in dollars, and the euro has strengthened sharply. What should the project manager do?

  • AReduce the scope immediately so that the cost stays inside the approved budget
  • BWait until the invoices arrive and then request more funding
  • CAsk the vendor to absorb the exchange loss as a sign of goodwill
  • DApply the plan's currency fluctuation procedure and update the forecast
Show the answer

Answer: D. The financial management plan sets a procedure for currency fluctuations, such as allowances, fixed-rate contracting or hedging through finance, and the forecast is updated. Asking for goodwill, waiting for invoices or cutting scope on impulse skips that procedure.

S8On a hybrid project, the team finds in-scope work that was never estimated, a required safety test, and wants to draw on the management reserve. What is the correct handling?

  • ADraw on the management reserve directly, since the PM controls all reserves
  • BRequest it through the approval path, with a change request to update the baseline
  • CUse the contingency reserve, which exists to cover any unforeseen in-scope work that appears
  • DAbsorb the cost silently within the existing work package budgets
Show the answer

Answer: B. Management reserve covers unforeseen in-scope work and is released through the organization's approval path, usually by senior management, with a change request so the baseline reflects the new authorization. Contingency is for identified risks, and drawing it unilaterally or absorbing it silently hides the overrun.

S9Three accepted risks have these values: 20% chance of a 100,000 loss, 50% chance of a 40,000 loss and 10% chance of a 300,000 loss. About how much contingency do their expected monetary values suggest?

  • AAbout 30,000, the largest single expected monetary value
  • BAbout 23,000, the average of the three expected values
  • CAbout 70,000, the sum of the three expected monetary values
  • DAbout 440,000, the sum of the three full impacts of the risks
Show the answer

Answer: C. Each expected monetary value is probability times impact: 20,000, 20,000 and 30,000, and their sum of about 70,000 sizes the contingency before adjustments. The sum of full impacts overstates it, and the largest or average value understates the combined exposure.

S10Customers return defective units under warranty, even though the project spent heavily on inspections. Which cost category do the warranty repairs belong to?

  • AInternal failure, part of the cost of nonconformance
  • BAppraisal, part of the cost of conformance
  • CExternal failure, part of the cost of nonconformance
  • DPrevention, part of the cost of conformance
Show the answer

Answer: C. Warranty work arises from defects found by the customer, which is external failure within the cost of nonconformance. Inspections are appraisal, training and better processes are prevention, and internal failure covers defects the project finds itself.

12.2 Recall Q&As

R1Name the four Finance processes.

Show the answer

Plan Financial Management, Estimate Costs, Develop Budget, Monitor and Control Finances.

R2What does the financial management plan define?

Show the answer

Units of measure, precision, accuracy, links to the WBS and control accounts, control thresholds, EVM rules, reporting formats, and details such as funding choices, currency fluctuation procedure and cost recording.

R3Cost baseline, project budget and funding requirements?

Show the answer

The cost baseline is the approved time-phased budget excluding management reserve. The project budget may add reserves depending on practice. Funding requirements are total and periodic funds derived from the baseline; total funds equal the baseline plus management reserve.

R4Contingency reserve versus management reserve?

Show the answer

Contingency covers known risks with active responses and sits in or near the baseline; management reserve covers unforeseen in-scope work, lies outside the baseline and is usually released by senior management.

R5Name the funding strategies.

Show the answer

Fixed or reallocated internal budgets, lump sum, incremental disbursement, external investment, government or NGO grants, crowdfunding and client contract.

R6What are the categories of cost of quality?

Show the answer

Conformance (prevention and appraisal) and nonconformance (internal and external failure). An optimal level exists.

R7What is funding limit reconciliation?

Show the answer

Matching planned spending to funding limits, often by rescheduling work with imposed dates to level out expenditure.

R8Give CV and SV and their meaning.

Show the answer

CV = EV − AC (negative: over budget); SV = EV − PV (negative: behind schedule).

R9Give CPI and SPI.

Show the answer

CPI = EV ÷ AC; SPI = EV ÷ PV. Above 1 is favorable.

R10List the four EAC formulas.

Show the answer

BAC ÷ CPI; AC + (BAC − EV); AC + bottom-up ETC; AC + (BAC − EV) ÷ (CPI × SPI).

R11What are ETC and VAC?

Show the answer

ETC = EAC − AC (or a bottom-up reestimate); VAC = BAC − EAC.

R12What does TCPI tell you?

Show the answer

The cost efficiency needed on the remaining work to meet a goal: (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC), or with EAC in the denominator. Above 1 is harder, below 1 easier.

R13How is earned value used in adaptive projects?

Show the answer

In story points: PV = points planned to date, EV = points of stories done, AC = the team's cost for the iteration.

R14Why does the timing of cost measurement matter?

Show the answer

Cost can be recognized when committed, ordered, delivered or incurred; stakeholders differ, so the project defines the measurement point and aligns it with accounting.

13Quick Reference Card

Processes Plan Financial Management → Estimate Costs → Develop Budget → Monitor and Control Finances

Funding strategies Internal budgets, lump sum, incremental, external investment, grants, crowdfunding, client contract
